task_row_model.query: In the 2020 randomized controlled trial of mindfulness-based stress reduction (MBSR) for older adults, what were the randomized sample size, the inclusion and exclusion criteria, and the primary outcome effect size with its 95% confidence interval and p-value?

documents.content: Methods — The single-center, parallel-group randomized controlled trial enrolled 240 community-dwelling older adults in 2019–2020 and randomized them 1:1 to an 8-week mindfulness-based stress reduction (MBSR) program or an active health-education control (120 participants per arm). Eligible participants were aged 65–80 years, scored ≥24 on the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA), and had no history of major psychiatric disorder or neurodegenerative disease. The prespecified primary outcome was change from baseline to 8 weeks on an n-back working memory test administered by blinded assessors. Randomization used permuted blocks; analysis was intention-to-treat.
documents.reasoning_trace: Contains trial design, randomized sample size, inclusion criteria, primary outcome definition and timing; used for sample and inclusion facts.

documents.content: Results summary — Investigators reported a small-to-moderate improvement in working memory for MBSR versus control. The primary outcome yielded a standardized effect size (Cohen's d) of 0.42 with a 95% confidence interval of 0.15 to 0.69, and a two-sided p-value of 0.003 after adjusting for baseline score and site. The report noted the result remained significant in sensitivity analyses and framed the finding as clinically meaningful for cognitive aging. The news-style writeup included commentary from outside experts and comparisons to earlier, smaller mindfulness studies.
documents.reasoning_trace: Provides the trial's primary outcome effect size, 95% CI, and p-value; used for result extraction.

documents.content: Investigator notes — Screening logs and protocol appendices clarified exclusions: active meditation practice exceeding two sessions per week was an exclusion to avoid prior training confounds, as were severe visual or auditory impairments that would prevent valid cognitive testing. Attrition was modest and balanced between arms. The working memory task used in most sessions and assessments was the 3-back variant of the n-back test, scored as change in correct responses from baseline to 8 weeks. Field notes emphasize standardized training of assessors and that participants remained community-dwelling throughout follow-up.
documents.reasoning_trace: Supplies exclusion criteria (meditation frequency, sensory impairments) and specifies the n-back variant used; used to supplement measurement and exclusion information.

documents.content: Background — Mindfulness has a long cultural history dating back millennia, with countless case vignettes of stress reduction in nonclinical populations. Population surveys report varying meditation prevalence by country and decade; some commentators speculate about broad societal effects. Several unrelated case reports describe mindfulness in younger adults with anxiety disorders, and methodological debates continue about appropriate control conditions. While interesting historically, these tangential discussions do not alter core trial parameters such as randomization ratio or primary outcome metrics.

task_row_model.golden_answer: The trial randomized 240 community-dwelling older adults (120 per arm). Inclusion: age 65–80, MoCA ≥24, no major psychiatric disorder; exclusion: active meditation >2 sessions/week and severe visual or auditory impairment. Primary outcome was change on the 3-back n-back working memory test at 8 weeks; effect size Cohen's d = 0.42 (95% CI 0.15–0.69), p = 0.003.
